subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: planning for sustainability and handover [Thinking]
passage: Sunday. Been thinking about what happens to the evening reading circle if I take the Pune job next year, or just get swamped at work. Right now it's me: I hold the key, the booklist and the phone numbers. That isn't a project, it's a habit of mine. So this month I asked Minakshi, who lives two lanes from the hall and comes every day, to start opening up and leading the story hour. Showed how the register works, where the books go, who to call about the hall. Also asked five parents for a small monthly amount, enough for the hall's electricity bill. Four said yes. On Thursday Minakshi read to the kids alone while I stood outside. It wobbled, and it worked. — Manoj

qa.q: How many parents said yes to giving a small monthly amount?
qa.a: Four parents said yes.

qa.q: What is Manoj worried about?
qa.a: Manoj is worried that the reading circle depends on Manoj alone, so it is a personal habit and not yet a lasting project.

qa.q: What other step could help the circle carry on without Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj could write a one-page handover with the steps for opening up, the register and the hall contacts, so any volunteer could follow it.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt reading to the children alone while Manoj stood outside?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably nervous but trusted, since it wobbled and then worked.

grounding: Shows a person asking who will run the reading circle when they are busy or away, training a local volunteer and arranging small monthly funding.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: I'm Lalit. Three years ago, after a good bonus, I paid for a computer lab in a school in a district I'd read about. Twenty machines, new desks, a ribbon-cutting. I was proud. I had never asked the school what it needed. Power there went off for most of the day with no backup, and no one on the staff had been taught to use the machines. When I visited a year later, Pradeep, the headmaster, walked me into the room. The screens were under plastic sheets and the door was kept locked to protect them. He said the teachers would have preferred a roof that didn't leak. That stayed with me. I had made a gift that fitted my picture of help, not their school.

qa.q: How many machines were in the lab?
qa.a: There were twenty machines in the lab.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling at the ribbon-cutting, and how did it change at the later visit?
qa.a: Lalit felt proud at the ribbon-cutting, but at the later visit felt regretful and humbled on seeing the covered screens and locked door.

qa.q: What could Lalit have done differently before paying for the lab?
qa.a: Lalit could have asked the school what it needed and started small with backup power and teacher training, since a fit with the local situation decides whether equipment gets used.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt about the lab?
qa.a: Pradeep was probably grateful but frustrated, keeping the room locked to protect it and mentioning that teachers wanted a roof that didn't leak.

grounding: Shows a person funding a school computer lab without power backup or trained teachers, so the equipment sits unused.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: In a village hall outside Jhansi, Sachin ran a Saturday tuition centre for forty children. Every month he sat down with Preeti, a volunteer teacher, and a notebook. They counted attendance from the register, marked the short maths test, and asked each child for one line on what they liked and disliked. In March the reading circle had eleven children on average and scores had barely moved. The children's notes said, 'Story time is the best.' Maths practice had steady attendance and rising scores. The two decided: drop the drawing class, which had few children and no change in anything; change reading to use stories; keep maths as it was. Sachin pinned the numbers on the hall wall. 'We'll look again in April,' he said.

qa.q: How many children did the reading circle have on average in March?
qa.a: The reading circle had eleven children on average.

qa.q: What does Sachin want from looking at the numbers again in April?
qa.a: Sachin wants decisions to rest on evidence and to keep adjusting, which shows a steady commitment to the centre.

qa.q: What other kind of evidence could Sachin add to the monthly numbers?
qa.a: Sachin could ask parents at pick-up time what they notice at home, since families may see changes that scores and registers miss.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the decision to drop the drawing class?
qa.a: Preeti probably sees it as fair because the numbers back it, though may feel sorry for the few children who enjoyed it.

grounding: Shows an organiser recording attendance, test scores and student feedback each month and using them to decide whether to continue, adjust or stop each activity.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: transparent accounts and legal setup [Action]
passage:
'Before the donation drive, I want us registered properly,' said Lakshmi, putting a folder on Shreya's desk.
'Good,' said Shreya, a lawyer at the legal aid clinic. 'I'll draft the trust papers with you. And the bank account goes in the trust's name, not yours.'
'And every rupee goes in a ledger the same day?'
'Yes, with a receipt number. A chartered accountant should look at the books once a year.'
'Can donors see the accounts?'
'They should. A short summary on your page each quarter.'
Lakshmi hesitated. 'Won't some people think we're showing off?'
'People give more when they can see where it goes. And clear records help whenever the authorities ask.'
Lakshmi nodded and wrote on the folder: Ledger. Receipts. Quarterly summary.

qa.q: Whose name should the bank account be in?
qa.a: The bank account goes in the trust's name, not Lakshmi's.

qa.q: What worried Lakshmi about sharing the accounts?
qa.a: Lakshmi was worried that some people would think the trust was showing off.

qa.q: What other step could Lakshmi add to keep donors informed?
qa.a: Lakshmi could invite one donor each quarter to look over the ledger in person, since seeing the books first-hand builds trust.

qa.q: How might a donor see the quarterly summary?
qa.a: A donor would likely feel trusted and reassured, and more willing to give again, because they can see where the money goes. 🙂

grounding: Shows an organiser registering a trust with a lawyer's help, keeping clear records and sharing accounts with donors.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: balancing the project with job and health [Thinking]
passage:
Week twelve, Tuesday: Usha, a bank analyst, finished the day's work at nine, then spent until one in the morning on the literacy project's spreadsheets. Her eyes stung and her hands shook from too much tea. Next morning she missed a step at her desk, and that evening Ayesha, a volunteer, found her asleep at the project table.

Saturday: Usha sat with Ayesha and said, 'If I burn out, the project stops. It's only worth doing if I'm still here in two years.' She wrote a limit: Tuesday and Saturday, three hours each, and one week off every month.

Two weeks later: Usha put out a call on the neighbourhood group and six new people came. She left at eight on Tuesday, tired in a normal way, and for the first time did not check her phone.

qa.q: How many hours did Usha set for each of Tuesday and Saturday?
qa.a: Usha set three hours for each.

qa.q: What is Usha afraid of when saying 'If I burn out, the project stops'?
qa.a: Usha is afraid the project would collapse if she wore herself out, and she wants it to last longer than her energy.

qa.q: What other step could Usha take besides limiting her hours?
qa.a: Usha could hand the spreadsheets to one of the new volunteers, since sharing the late-night tasks protects both her health and the project.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt on finding Usha asleep at the table?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably worried and concerned, seeing how tired Usha had become.

grounding: Shows a person noticing burnout after months of late nights, limiting the project to fixed weekly hours and inviting more volunteers.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: After a year of Saturday coding classes in a community hall in Durban, Nour opened the attendance sheets with Lindiwe, a teacher at the local school. Forty-one children had come regularly. Six were girls. 'Why so few?' Nour asked. Lindiwe suggested asking the mothers, so they spent two weekends talking to families at the market and the bus rank. Several mothers said they wanted to know who ran the class before letting a daughter go, and Saturday afternoons were when girls were needed at home. Nour moved the class to Saturday morning, invited mothers to sit in on the first session, and asked a woman teacher, Thandi, to co-lead. Three months later the attendance sheet showed seventeen girls.

qa.q: How many of the regular children were girls after the first year?
qa.a: Six of the forty-one regular children were girls.

qa.q: What was Nour feeling when looking at the sheet?
qa.a: Nour was puzzled and concerned, shown by asking, 'Why so few?'

qa.q: What other approach could Nour use to learn more about why girls stayed away?
qa.a: Nour could also have a short chat with girls themselves, since their reasons may differ from what their mothers say.

qa.q: How might the mothers have seen the invitation to sit in?
qa.a: Several mothers were probably reassured, since they wanted to know who ran the class before letting a daughter go.

grounding: Shows a person using a year of attendance data to see that weekend classes reach few girls, and adding a timing and a woman teacher after hearing from mothers.

subtype: Approach: starts from the finished picture and asks what comes just before it [Thinking]
passage: Teacher's note. Salma, five, held up the picture from the box and said, 'This is what I want.' She pointed to the tower's tip and asked me, 'What goes on top?' 'A small red one,' I said. 'And under the red one?' She traced down the picture with her finger, saying, 'Yellow, then green,' to the bottom. Then she picked the two big blue blocks first and set them on the floor. Mahima, sitting beside her, wanted to begin with the tall ones, so Salma showed her the picture. I only handed out blocks. The tower stood.

qa.q: What went on top of the tower?
qa.a: A small red block went on top.

qa.q: What does Salma want?
qa.a: Salma wants her tower to look like the one in the picture, and she is eager and careful, checking each block against it.

qa.q: What could Salma do if the tower fell over?
qa.a: Salma could look at the picture again and start once more from the big blue blocks at the bottom.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt when Salma showed her the picture?
qa.a: Mahima probably felt curious, since she wanted to start with the tall ones and then saw a reason for starting with the base.

grounding: Shows a child looking at the picture of the finished tower and asking what goes on top and then what goes under it, so the base blocks are chosen first.

subtype: Approach: counts back from a fixed date to set small deadlines [Action]
passage: Kavya's school in a village near Nashik had its science fair on Friday. On Saturday evening she sat on the veranda with the calendar and counted backwards on her fingers. 'Fair is Friday. Poster ready Thursday, so Chetan Sir can see it. Experiment on Tuesday, in case it goes wrong. Materials before that, so I buy them Sunday when Papa goes to the market.' She put the days on separate sticky notes: Sun buy, Tue experiment, Thu poster, and stuck them on her desk. On Tuesday the first try failed, but she still had two days to fix it. On Friday the poster was dry and the experiment worked.

qa.q: On which day did Kavya plan to run the experiment?
qa.a: Kavya planned the 'Experiment on Tuesday', in case it goes wrong.

qa.q: What did Kavya want to leave time for by running the experiment on Tuesday?
qa.a: Kavya wanted time to fix it if it went wrong, which shows she was a little worried about it failing.

qa.q: What other approach could help Kavya keep to her dates?
qa.a: Kavya could ask Papa or Chetan Sir to look at her sticky notes on Wednesday, since a check-in shows early if something is behind.

qa.q: How might Chetan Sir see Kavya's plan?
qa.a: Chetan Sir probably sees a student who manages her time well, since the poster was ready before the fair.

grounding: Shows a girl counting back from Friday to set the dates for the poster, the experiment and buying materials, and marking each on a sticky note.

subtype: Approach: fixes the target score and derives weekly study targets from it [Thinking]
passage:
Hi Vaibhav bhaiya,

You asked how the Class 11 physics plan is going, so here it is. The paper is out of 70, so 90 percent means 63. Mechanics carries 20 marks and my last test gave me only 11 there, and Optics is the same story, so those two decide everything. The exam is 14 weeks away. I've set two chapters a week, 25 problems per chapter, Mechanics and Optics first, and a timed test every Sunday. Mumma says it looks like a railway timetable 😅 but I feel calmer. Can you check whether 25 problems is too many? I can't tell.

Anjali

qa.q: How many marks does 90 percent of the paper make?
qa.a: Ninety percent of the paper makes 63 marks.

qa.q: How does Anjali feel about the plan?
qa.a: Anjali feels calmer with the plan, even though Mumma jokes that it looks like a railway timetable. 🙂

qa.q: What could Anjali do if the weekly targets start to slip?
qa.a: Anjali could ask a teacher which problem types matter most for the exam and shrink the count on strong topics, so time goes to the weak units.

qa.q: How does Mumma see the plan?
qa.a: Mumma is amused, joking that it looks like a railway timetable, and probably notices how strict it is.

grounding: Shows a student fixing a target score in physics, estimating the marks needed per unit and setting weekly chapter and problem counts from the exam date.

subtype: Approach: assumes only the last step is known and chains backwards [Pitfall]
passage: In her hostel room in Bengaluru, Shalini drew the chain on a sheet: 'Job at a product company' at the top, and beneath it 'crack the final interview', then 'clear the online test', then 'strong project on my resume'. Neat arrows all the way down. She showed it to Lalit, a classmate. 'What's the first box?' he asked. She pointed at the bottom one: 'Get better at coding.' 'Better how? By when? With what?' She shrugged; the arrows looked so tidy she had never asked. Weeks went by. The sheet stayed on the wall and she felt organised, but her practice was scattered, a few videos here, a few problems there. At the online test in October she found she had never checked whether two months was enough. She fell short.

qa.q: What was the first box in Shalini's chain?
qa.a: The first box was 'Get better at coding'.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about her chain of boxes?
qa.a: Shalini felt organised and comfortable because the arrows looked tidy, but she had no answer when asked about the first box.

qa.q: What could Shalini do to make the first step real?
qa.a: Shalini could set a concrete first target, such as thirty problems a week on one topic, and ask a senior whether the timeline is realistic.

qa.q: How might Lalit see her chart?
qa.a: Lalit probably sees a tidy chart with a vague base, which is why he asked how, by when and with what.

grounding: Shows a student who chains backwards from a product-company job but never checks whether the early steps are achievable, so the first step stays vague.
